podcasts.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
podcasts.summary:
Paul Christiano
is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen).
Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario).
He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails.
He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it.
And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this pr

"When you ask Claude to create something, it's operating in a fresh context where it thinks: Oh my God, the user asked me to make an app. I'm going to invent the most brilliant visual style."

From @nateparrott at Anthropic on how to get Claude to avoid the same designs:

"It's going to be serif text, an off-white background, orange, and these bars on the edges of the cards. Because in Claude's mind, it's only ever done this once, so it thinks this is totally original.

So in our Claude Design prompt, we tell Claude, 'For this particular model, you tend to overly bias toward these two fonts and colors. So don't use them unless the user asks you to.' That tends to help a lot."

📌 Watch our full episode here: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX

"Do you find being a designer more fun now that you can easily prototype everything?"

That's the question I asked @nateparrott (Anthropic). His answer:

"I'm a little weird in that I have an engineering background. Before Anthropic, I worked at The Browser Company, where we made a browser called Arc.

We spent a year in pre-production before we released Arc. It took us a couple weeks to build out each idea and see which worked.

Now at Anthropic, you can kind of do that in one to two days.

So you've really compressed the cycle of building. What you haven't compressed is the cycle of putting it in people's hands and understanding if they're going to use it."

Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf.

A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser, network, filesystem, system fonts. Renders a post to PNG in ~1ms (and 0.4 ms for @jack's "setting up my twttr" 😁).

X is the global town square, and the medium is the message. Being able to preview what things will look like before posting is great for both humans and agents.

Rendering with xeet is is 100x-1000x faster than booting up a browser and taking a screenshot, yet it's just as accurate.

It reproduces Blink & HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64px line breaking, RTL bidi, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK/Math/Emoji fallbacks, "Show more" rules, etc. It's the kind of thing that would be wildly impractical, if not impossible, for a human engineer to pull off.

Except 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝 is structured as an "autorepo." An oracle boots up Chrome, and verifies tens of thousands of text layout rules. A CI canary then watches the evolution of the original, and files signed PRs for agents to act on. It was conceived from the ground up around 'verification engineering', and the result speaks for itself.

Enjoy!
